name: AI for School and Educational Leaders 1: Introduction to AI in Education
objectives: When a staff member, parent or student asks what AI is, explain AI and generative AI in plain words, including why it can be wrong, in two sentences a new teacher, a parent and a fifth grader could understand

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What AI is, in words your staff will use
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain AI and generative AI to staff in plain words.
This lesson builds toward: When a staff member, parent or student asks what AI is, you will explain AI and generative AI in plain words, including why it can be wrong, in two sentences a new teacher, a parent and a fifth grader could understand.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is software that does tasks that usually need human judgment, such as recognizing speech, spotting patterns or writing. Generative AI creates new content: text, images, audio and code. Chat tools such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini and Claude are built on large language models (LLMs) that predict likely words.
Because they predict likely words, these tools write fluently and can still be wrong, out of date or biased. They do not know your students, your curriculum or your community unless someone tells them, and they should not be told private student information.
A simple way to say it to staff: "AI is a fast first-draft partner. It does not replace the teacher's judgment, and it is never the final word on a student."
Words to know:
- Generative AI: AI that creates new text, images, audio or code.
- LLM: large language model: the AI behind chat assistants.
- Hallucination: when AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
Try it now: Write a two-sentence explanation of AI that a new teacher, a parent and a fifth grader could all understand. Test it on one colleague.
You can now explain AI and generative AI in plain words to staff and families.

options: AI that creates new text, images or code
A program that grades tests automatically
A search engine for school records
Software that never makes mistakes
check.why: Generative AI creates new content, which is why it can also produce errors.

check.q: A parent asks why a chatbot gave their child a wrong fact. What would you explain?
options: The child must have typed it wrong
AI predicts likely words and can be wrong, so its answers need checking
The tool was broken that day
Only paid AI tools are accurate
check.why: AI predicts likely text instead of checking facts, so it can sound right and still be wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Where AI already shows up in your school
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Map where AI is already used in your school, officially and unofficially.
This lesson builds toward: With your tech coordinator or two teachers, you will map where AI already shows up in your school, listing at least six places, each marked approved or not and whether it touches student data.
AI is already in your building. Teachers may use chat tools to draft lessons or parent emails. Students may use them for homework, sometimes appropriately, sometimes not. Many products your district already pays for (learning platforms, writing tools, reading programs, office software) have added AI features, sometimes switched on by default.
There is also AI behind the scenes: adaptive practice programs that pick the next question, early-warning dashboards, plagiarism and AI-writing detectors, and security or monitoring tools.
Leaders cannot guide what they cannot see. A quick map, built with your tech coordinator and a few teachers, shows which tools are approved, which are being used anyway, and which touch student data. That map is the starting point for every later decision.
Step by step:
- Ask teachers, students and your tech coordinator which AI tools they use.
- List AI features inside products you already have.
- Mark each: approved or not, and whether it touches student data.
- Note where students meet AI without knowing it.
Words to know:
- Adaptive program: software that changes the next question or activity based on a student's answers.
- AI-writing detector: a tool that claims to tell whether text was written by AI; often unreliable.
Try it now: With your tech coordinator or two teachers, list at least six places AI shows up in your school. Mark each approved or not, and whether it touches student data.
You can now map where AI is already used in your school and which uses touch student data.

check.q: What is an adaptive learning program?
options: A program teachers change by hand each day
A program that works without internet
A program that changes the next activity based on a student's answers
A program that only adults can use
check.why: Adaptive programs use a student's answers to choose what comes next.

check.q: You learn that a tool your school already owns has a new AI feature switched on. What would you do?
options: Ignore it, since the tool was already approved
Ban the whole tool at once
Ask teachers to stop using computers
Add it to your AI map and check whether it touches student data
check.why: AI features can appear in tools you already own, so they belong on the map.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Where AI helps learning, and where it harms
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort school uses of AI into helpful, careful and harmful.
This lesson builds toward: Given AI uses seen in schools, you will sort each use into helpful, careful or harmful, with one reason for each, using the family test.
Helpful uses usually save teacher time or widen access: drafting lesson materials, creating practice questions at several reading levels, translating family letters for a qualified person to check, and giving students a patient tutor-like explainer under teacher guidance.
Careful uses need clear rules: students using AI on assignments (it can replace the thinking the assignment was meant to build), AI feedback on student work (it can be generic or wrong), and AI-writing detectors (they can wrongly accuse students, including English learners).
Harmful uses: entering student personal information into unapproved tools, letting AI make decisions about grades, placement, discipline or special education, and using AI in ways families were not told about. A test for staff: "Would I be comfortable explaining this use to the student's family?"
Words to know:
- Access: whether every student can take part and benefit, including students with disabilities and English learners.
- False accusation: wrongly saying a student cheated, for example because a detector flagged their work.
Try it now: List eight AI uses you have seen or heard of in schools. Mark each HELPFUL, CAREFUL or HARMFUL and write one reason.
You can now judge which school uses of AI help learning and which put students at risk.

check.q: What does the family test ask?
options: Would I explain this AI use to the student's family?
Does the family own a computer?
Did the family pay for the tool?
Would the family use AI at home?
check.why: If you would not explain it to a family, the use needs a second look.

check.q: A teacher wants to use an AI detector to decide whether essays were cheated. How would you mark it?
options: HELPFUL: it saves time
HARMFUL: AI should never be used
CAREFUL: detectors can wrongly accuse students, so they are never the only evidence
Not worth discussing
check.why: Detectors can wrongly accuse students, including English learners.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: What leaders must know first

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Student privacy basics: FERPA and COPPA
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: State the FERPA and COPPA basics that apply when staff use AI tools.
This lesson builds toward: When staff use AI tools, you will state the FERPA and COPPA basics and rewrite a request so it contains no student information, naming when to ask your privacy officer or legal counsel.
FERPA, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, protects the privacy of students' education records: records directly related to a student and kept by the school. Parents have the right to inspect and review those records and ask for corrections; the rights move to the student at 18 or when they attend college. Schools generally need consent to disclose personally identifiable information, with exceptions such as directory information (after notice and a chance to opt out) and school officials with a legitimate educational interest. An outside vendor can count as a school official only if it performs a school service, is under the school's direct control, and follows limits on re-sharing.
COPPA, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, enforced by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), protects children under 13 online. The FTC says a school may give consent in place of parents only when the service collects information for the use and benefit of the school and for no other commercial purpose. The FTC amended its COPPA Rule on April 22, 2025.
What this means in practice: a teacher who pastes student names, grades, IEP details or other identifying information into a free AI tool the district has not approved may be disclosing education records to a company with no agreement. The leader's rule: only district-approved tools for anything about students, and remove identifying details anyway. For your exact obligations, ask your district's privacy officer or counsel; state student-privacy laws may add more.
Words to know:
- FERPA: the federal law that protects the privacy of student education records.
- COPPA: the federal law that protects the online privacy of children under 13.
- Personally identifiable information (PII): information that identifies a student, such as name, ID number or a mix of details.
- Directory information: basic details like name and dates of attendance that a school may share after notice and opt-out.
Official sources:
- FERPA: Protecting Student Privacy (US Department of Education)
- FTC: Complying with COPPA, Frequently Asked Questions
- FTC: Children's Privacy
Try it now: Write three examples of what a teacher must NOT paste into an unapproved AI tool, and rewrite one of them so it asks for the same help without any student information.
You can now state the FERPA and COPPA basics that apply to staff AI use and the rule that follows from them.

options: Teachers' email accounts
The online privacy of children under 13
School buildings
Student sports records only
check.why: COPPA protects the online privacy of children under 13.

check.q: A teacher wants AI help writing feedback for a named student with a low grade. What would you suggest?
options: Paste the name and grade into any free tool
Use the student's initials instead, which is always safe
Skip feedback for that student
Ask for help with the feedback without any student name or grade, or use a district-approved tool
check.why: Removing student information, or using an approved tool, protects the education record.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: What federal guidance says about AI in schools
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Summarize federal AI guidance and find the current version yourself.
This lesson builds toward: Given federal and state guidance on AI in schools, you will summarize one federal principle and find your state's current guidance, noting its date and one point it makes, or that none exists yet.
On July 22, 2025, the US Department of Education sent a Dear Colleague Letter on AI. As reported by K-12 Dive, it says existing federal grant funds may support AI used for high-quality curriculum tools, high-impact tutoring, and college and career pathway advising, and it sets out principles: AI initiatives should be educator-led, ethical, accessible to students with disabilities, transparent about how new tools are rolled out, and compliant with federal data privacy laws.
Guidance changes. Read the letter itself and any newer guidance on ed.gov, and check what your state education agency has published; many states have their own AI guidance for schools. The Department's Student Privacy Policy Office site (studentprivacy.ed.gov) has resources on online educational services, including a Model Terms of Service checklist.
For leaders, the principles are a useful test for any AI plan: Is it educator-led? Is it accessible? Have we told families how it works? Does it protect student data?
Step by step:
- Read the Department of Education's AI letter on ed.gov.
- Check your state education agency for AI guidance.
- Look at studentprivacy.ed.gov resources on online educational services.
- Test your plans against the principles: educator-led, ethical, accessible, transparent, privacy-compliant.
Words to know:
- Dear Colleague Letter: a guidance letter from a federal agency to schools and states; guidance, not a new law.
- State education agency: your state's department of education.
Official sources:
- K-12 Dive: Education Department issues AI priorities (July 2025)
- Privacy and Education Technology (Student Privacy Policy Office)
Try it now: Find your state education agency's page on AI (search its website for "artificial intelligence"). Write down the date of its latest guidance and one point it makes, or note that none exists yet.
You can now summarize federal AI guidance for schools and find the current federal and state versions.

check.q: Where do you look for your state's AI guidance for schools?
options: Your state education agency's website
A social media post
The AI tool's own answer
A vendor's sales page
check.why: The state education agency is the official source for state guidance.

check.q: A colleague quotes federal AI guidance from memory. What would you do before sharing it with staff?
options: Share it, since it sounds right
Find the current official document and check its date and wording
Ask an AI chatbot to confirm it
Wait for another colleague to agree
check.why: Guidance changes, so leaders check the current official version themselves.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Opening the AI conversation with your staff
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Lead a 15-minute staff conversation on AI using a one-page handout.
This lesson builds toward: With your staff, you will lead a 15-minute AI conversation using a one-page "AI at our school" handout, with every handout part included and the top three staff questions recorded.
Staff feel many things about AI: excitement, worry about cheating, fear of being replaced, or simply too busy to care. Open with listening, not a policy. Ask: "Where have you seen AI this year, in your class or your own life?"
Then share a one-page handout: what AI is in two sentences, three ways it can help teachers, three risks for students, the privacy rule, and who to ask. Keep it to one page; you can add detail later.
Close by naming one next step (for example, a short survey of tools staff use, or a volunteer group of teachers to test an approved tool) and collect the top questions. Those questions tell you what to teach next.
Step by step:
- Open with a listening question.
- Share the one-page handout.
- Discuss one helpful and one risky example.
- Name one next step.
- Collect the top three questions.
Words to know:
- Handout: a short printed or shared page that people keep.
- Next step: one clear action the group agrees to take.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page "AI at our school" handout (two-sentence definition, three helps, three risks, privacy rule, who to ask). Lead a 15-minute staff conversation with it and record the top three questions staff raised.
You can now open and lead your school's conversation about AI with a clear, shared starting point.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Plain definition The definition uses jargon or is longer than two sentences. Explains AI in two plain sentences. A colleague who is new to AI understood it on first reading. Helps and risks Fewer than three helps or three risks, or they do not fit school. Three ways AI can help teachers and three risks for students. Each risk says what staff should do about it. Privacy rule The privacy rule is missing or unclear. States that no student names, grades or other personally identifiable information go into AI tools the district has not approved. Gives a short example of asking for help without student information. Who to ask Does not say who to ask. Names who to ask with questions. Also names the privacy officer for privacy questions. Staff conversation No conversation held, or questions not recorded. Led a 15-minute conversation and recorded the top three questions. Ended with one clear next step for staff. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a good way to open a staff conversation on AI?
options: Announce a list of bans
Show a long slide deck on how AI works
Ask a listening question about where staff have seen AI
Start with a quiz
check.why: Starting by listening shows staff their experience matters.

check.q: At the end of your 15-minute conversation, staff still have many questions. What do you do?
options: Answer every one, even if it runs an hour
Tell them to search online
End without a next step
Record the top three questions and give one next step
check.why: A clear next step and the collected questions shape what you do next.
